newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin makes daughter official image adviser.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin makes daughter official image adviser.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, who celebrates the first anniversary of his re-election this week, finally gave official credit to the daughter who helped keep him in the Kremlin by naming her his official image-maker on Monday.
"By decree of the president...Tatyana Borisovna Dyachenko is named adviser to the president," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky intoned drily during a routine news briefing.
Asked what precisely the 37-year-old Tatyana would advise her father on, he replied simply: "The president's image."
The announcement had long been expected. The blonde computer mathematician and mother-of-two is a fixture in the Kremlin, providing her father with a "reality check" among his advisers.
"It's just easier for me to tell him what others can't," Dyachenko was quoted telling Itar-Tass news agency, adding she would play a similar role to the one she had during the election campaign.
"His mistakes are more painful for me," she said, adding that she had no personal ambitions of her own.

First deputy prime minister and former Yeltsin campaign chief Anatoly Chubais said a month ago Dyachenko would provide a "common sense" antidote to Kremlin politicking. He also denied widespread rumours that he was the president's daughter's lover.
Dyachenko, whose younger son Gleb was born in 1995, joined Chubais's team in the dark early days of the campaign in 1996.

She was credited with helping the liberal Chubais persuade Yeltsin to ditch several hawkish aides -- including bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov, who is her son Gleb's godfather. Korzhakov has since turned bitterly against Yeltsin and his family.

Dyachenko helped soften a presidential image coarsened by the war in Chechnya. She reportedly ordered his bodyguards to take off sunglasses she said made them look like mobsters and was always on hand to touch up her father's trademark quiff.

When he fell ill days before his re-election and then spent months convalescing from multiple heart bypass surgery in November, Kremlin aides said Tatyana and Chubais were the ubiquitous gatekeepers of the 66-year-old president.
Dyachenko, though quick to welcome her father's move to end confusion about her role, said she was bracing for criticism.

"It removes any ambiguity from my position," she was quoted telling Russian news agencies, saying it had nonetheless been a difficult step for Yeltsin to take. "I'm morally prepared for people writing unkind -- and untrue -- things about my work."
Her close association with Chubais -- whose young team of economic reformers she praised on Monday -- has earned her the hostility of the communist and nationalist opposition.
Kremlin sources said one of the reasons the announcement was made now was that the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament began its summer recess last week.
Yeltsin faced charges of nepotism earlier this year after the husband of his elder daughter Yelena was named head of the state airline, Aeroflot.

Dyachenko has taken tips from Claude Chirac, daughter of the French president, who advises her father. Dyachenko noted the younger Chirac had had her critics in France and she appeared to anticipate some negative reaction in Russia.
But she cited as evidence of her legitimate contribution to the Kremlin the success of the election on July 3 last year.
She said her job would last three years -- until the next presidential election in the year 2000 when Yeltsin will retire.

Married to Alexei Dyachenko, she was born in the Urals city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, where Yeltsin was to become Communist party chief. While at university in Moscow in 1981 she gave birth to a son by a first husband. Now at school in England, the teenager has his grandfather's name, Boris Yeltsin.
